topics.chapterTitle: Performing Low-Level File and Device I/O
topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Low-level I/O reports byte counts and errors rather than automatically delivering complete records. A file may return fewer bytes than requested, and a successful write is not the same as durable storage. This Linux chapter writes a small private fixture, reads it through a descriptor, and maps it read-only. It does not access hardware device registers or arbitrary device files; those require separate platform-specific interfaces and authorization.

blocks.text: A log processor opens a file, reads a block, and treats a short read as a complete record. It passes its small demonstration because the file fits in one block. When the same parser is placed behind a pipe, records arrive in pieces and the interpretation fails. The defect is not that Linux lost bytes. The program confused one transfer operation with one application message.

blocks.text: This chapter separates object ownership, byte transfer, record interpretation, and storage persistence. A descriptor tells you which open resource an operation addresses. A returned count tells you how much progress occurred. A parser decides whether the accumulated bytes form a complete object. A durability policy decides when acknowledged output is expected to survive a failure. None of these responsibilities disappears when the interface is reduced to a short function call.

topics.title: 11.1.1 Opening and Closing Files
topics.summary: open selects access mode and behavior flags and returns a descriptor or an error. Creation requires an explicit permission mode, and flags such as exclusive creation can prevent accidental replacement of an existing file. Close-on-exec behavior limits unintended descriptor inheritance into a later process image. Adopt a successful descriptor into an owner immediately.

blocks.text: Opening a file establishes an open file description and returns a process-local descriptor referring to it. The description contains state such as the current offset and access mode; the descriptor has its own relevant flags, including close-on-exec. Duplicated descriptors can refer to the same open description and therefore share an offset. Copying an integer does not create an independent open operation or an independent resource owner. (OPEN)

blocks.text: Select access and creation flags deliberately. A reader generally does not need write access. Creating a new sensitive file calls for an explicit mode, with the understanding that the process umask can further restrict that mode. The worked example uses exclusive creation so an existing path is not silently truncated. Its fixture runner supplies a fresh temporary working directory; the filename alone would not establish a safe location in an arbitrary production directory.

blocks.text: Use close-on-exec at acquisition where the platform supports it. Opening first and setting the flag later leaves a window in which another thread could create a child process that inherits the resource. Linux’s O_CLOEXEC and corresponding socket or pipe facilities avoid that specific acquisition race. The choice protects the intended process boundary; it does not automatically close copies deliberately inherited through other mechanisms.

blocks.text: A pathname can change after a descriptor is opened. The demonstration unlinks its temporary name while retaining the open descriptor. Subsequent descriptor operations still address the open file. This is useful for a scoped scratch file, but it should not be mistaken for secure deletion, a portable replacement strategy, or permission to remove another application’s pathname. The fixture owns both the directory and the created file.

blocks.text: Closing releases the descriptor reference. On Linux, a close error must not be handled by blindly retrying the same integer, because the number may already have been released and reused. The supplied owner invalidates its stored descriptor before performing a checked close. It can report the error without later accidentally closing another resource. These are Linux-specific semantics; review another platform’s contract before transplanting the wrapper. (POSIXCLOSE)

topics.title: 11.1.2 Reading and Writing Raw Bytes
topics.summary: read and write return the number of bytes transferred, which can be smaller than requested. A loop must advance by actual progress and distinguish interruption, end-of-file, and other errors. A zero read indicates end-of-file for an ordinary stream-like file interface; a partial record followed by EOF is different from a clean end before any new record.

blocks.text: A successful write means bytes were accepted by the interface, not necessarily committed to durable storage. Filesystems, caches, and devices add persistence semantics. When durability is required, use the appropriate synchronization and error-checking protocol. Raw device I/O can impose additional alignment, ordering, and safety constraints that this regular-file example does not establish.

blocks.text: A successful read or write can transfer fewer bytes than requested. A correct loop advances by the returned count and works only on the remaining region. Returning the number of bytes actually transferred is not an inconvenience to hide: it is how the interface communicates progress across files, pipes, sockets, and other resources. The maximum request must also fit the interface’s representable count and platform limits. The book uses deliberately small bounded buffers. (POSIXIO, WRITE)

blocks.text: Distinguish an empty result from a failed operation. For a nonzero read request on a regular file or stream, zero conventionally signals end-of-file. A negative return reports an error through errno. Capture that error before unrelated calls can replace it. An interrupted call with no progress can often be retried, but a successful partial transfer has already changed the operation’s state and must be accounted for rather than replayed from the beginning.

blocks.text: An exact-read helper needs more than a Boolean success notion internally. Clean end-of-stream before a new record is different from end-of-stream halfway through a header or body. The shared helper returns false when no requested bytes were obtained before EOF, and throws for a truncated partial read. Its callers must decide whether that initial EOF is expected at that protocol point. A zero-length request is already complete; it should not be interpreted as evidence that the peer closed.

blocks.text: Blocking behavior belongs in the contract. A loop that correctly handles partial progress can still wait forever for the remainder. A per-call timeout can be repeatedly renewed by a peer that makes tiny progress. A total deadline requires carrying one absolute end time through all the reads and waits that constitute the operation. The extended server appendix makes this distinction executable rather than claiming that the elementary helper already solves it.

blocks.text: Writes also have an external-effect boundary. Once a prefix has been accepted by the kernel, throwing an exception cannot retract it. A retry at a higher layer can duplicate output unless the protocol supplies identifiers, acknowledgement rules, or idempotent operations. For a file, an accepted write does not by itself prove crash durability. Define whether the application promises merely to submit bytes, to finish a logical record, or to complete a persistence protocol.

topics.title: 11.2.1 Understanding Memory-Mapped I/O
topics.summary: mmap can map a file region into a process address space so ordinary memory accesses read or modify the mapping under its permissions and sharing mode. Mapping offsets and lengths have platform requirements, and failure is represented by MAP_FAILED rather than a null pointer. A mapping has its own lifetime and must be released with munmap.

blocks.text: File-backed mappings are not the same as device memory-mapped registers. Device mappings can require special access semantics and kernel-driver coordination. Even ordinary file mappings can fault if the underlying file is truncated by another actor. Establish ownership and mutation constraints before treating a mapped region as a stable byte sequence.

blocks.text: Memory mapping associates a region of virtual address space with a file or other supported object. A read-only mapping lets ordinary loads access the mapped bytes, but it does not turn arbitrary bytes into arbitrary C++ objects. Alignment, object lifetime, valid representations, endianness, and format constraints still apply. Treat mapped file content as bytes and decode the file format explicitly unless a much narrower representation contract has been established. (MMAP, LIFETIME)

blocks.text: A mapping owns a different resource from the descriptor used to create it. Closing the descriptor after a successful mapping does not normally remove the mapping on Linux, and destroying the mapping does not close an unrelated descriptor. Use separate owners with explicit lifetime relationships. Any span or string view into mapped storage is borrowed and becomes unusable when the mapping is removed, regardless of whether its pointer value still looks plausible.

blocks.text: Length and offset require validation. An empty file should be handled explicitly rather than passed as a zero-length mapping request. Mapping offsets must satisfy the platform’s alignment requirements. A window into a large file may therefore map from an earlier aligned offset and expose only the requested subrange. Check the arithmetic that combines the aligned offset, leading adjustment, and requested length before requesting address space.

blocks.text: The file can change independently of your pointer. If another actor truncates a mapped file, later accesses can generate a fault such as SIGBUS on Linux. Bounds checked against the original size do not protect against every concurrent filesystem mutation. Choose a stability policy: a private immutable input, coordination with writers, versioned files, or a copied snapshot. The teaching example controls its own scratch file and performs no concurrent truncation.

blocks.text: MAP_PRIVATE does not mean that the application receives a permanently frozen snapshot of every future external modification. It selects private copy-on-write behavior for writes through the mapping; broader visibility and stability questions still need a documented file-sharing contract. Likewise, unmapping releases an address-space resource, not a durability acknowledgement. A writable mapping requires a separately designed synchronization and persistence policy.

Closing the descriptor after a successful mapping does not normally remove the mapping on Linux, and destroying the mapping does not close an unrelated descriptor. Use separate owners with explicit lifetime relationships. Any span or string view into mapped storage is borrowed and becomes unusable when the mapping is removed, regardless of whether its pointer value still looks plausible.

Length and offset require validation. An empty file should be handled explicitly rather than passed as a zero-length mapping request. Mapping offsets must satisfy the platform’s alignment requirements. A window into a large file may therefore map from an earlier aligned offset and expose only the requested subrange. Check the arithmetic that combines the aligned offset, leading adjustment, and requested length before requesting address space.

The file can change independently of your pointer. If another actor truncates a mapped file, later accesses can generate a fault such as SIGBUS on Linux. Bounds checked against the original size do not protect against every concurrent filesystem mutation. Choose a stability policy: a private immutable input, coordination with writers, versioned files, or a copied snapshot. The teaching example controls its own scratch file and performs no concurrent truncation.

MAP_PRIVATE does not mean that the application receives a permanently frozen snapshot of every future external modification. It selects private copy-on-write behavior for writes through the mapping; broader visibility and stability questions still need a documented file-sharing contract. Likewise, unmapping releases an address-space resource, not a durability acknowledgement. A writable mapping requires a separately designed synchronization and persistence policy.

The reconstructed result must be identical. Then end the sequence before any byte, halfway through a header, and halfway through a body. Give each termination a documented outcome rather than allowing default-initialized fields to hide truncation.

blocks.text: Review reasoning. Does one successful read imply a complete application message? No. Does unlinking an owned temporary filename immediately invalidate its open descriptor? No. Does a mapped pointer outlive its mapping owner? No. Does a successful write establish survival after power loss? Not by itself. Why preserve partial progress? Because accepted bytes are an external effect that cannot safely be replayed as though nothing happened.
